previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis was admitted for severe joint pain following a gastrointestinal flare, unresponsive to oral steroids and pain medications. He was treated with IV methylprednisolone and IV analgesics, with successful transition to oral prednisone and home pain regimen as symptoms improved. MRI showed mild tenosynovitis without erosions, confirming active inflammatory arthritis. His diabetes and hypertension were managed with home medications. He was discharged home on a prednisone taper with instructions to follow up with rheumatology.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo M with a history of psoriatic arthritis, morbid obesity, 
HTN, DM2, presents with edema and pain in the left hand and knee 
consistent with previous arthritis exacerbations, without fever 
or systemic symptoms.  
.  
# Joint pain and swelling: At first, the patient's symptoms were 
felt to be related to an exacerbation of his psoriatic 
arthritis. There was no fever, leukocytosis, or systemic 
symptoms to suggest infection. The rheumatology service was 
consulted and performed arthrocentesis of the left knee on 
___. Gram stain was negative, and culture was also negative. 
The patient was treated with IV solumedrol, with no improvement 
in his symptoms.  It was noticed that, in general, purple and 
blue, patchy bruising followed the erythema, first in his left 
knee and three days later in his left shin.  There was concern 
for cellulitis of the left shin, and an infectious disease 
service was consulted.  The patient remained afebrile and the 
pattern of erythema and bruising was determined not to be 
consistent with infection.  He also received azathioprine 
according to his home regimen. The patient's pain was initially 
treated with IV Dilaudid, along with the patient's home regimen 
of gabapentin, indomethacin, lidocaine patch, MS ___, 
tizanidine, and nortriptyline. Oxycodone was decreased from the 
patient's preadmission dose of ___ mg Q4H PRN to 10 mg Q4H PRN 
in the setting of Dilaudid use, but this was changed to oral MS 
___ and Morphine ___. The patient continued azathioprine 
according to his home regimen. He received Bactrim for PCP 
___. The patient was discharged on prednisone 60mg PO 
daily to be tapered by 10mg per week.
.

- Continued home lisinopril, Toprol XL, HCTZ, aspirin, and 
atorvastatin.
.  
# Diabetes mellitis, type 2: Continued glargine at the patient's 
preadmission dose. The patient counted carbohydrates and managed 
his own Humalog insulin sliding scale.

# Osteoporosis: Likely secondary to steroid use. Continued 
alendronate, calcium, and vitamin D.

Discharge Instructions:
You came to the hospital with pain in your left knee and left 
hand. You had some fluid removed from your left knee, which did 
not show any infection. You were treated with IV steroids for 
your arthritis, with some improvement in your symptoms.  An MRI 
of your left knee showed that there was fluid in your knee and 
that you had a small tear in the meniscus.  You continued to 
have swelling and redness in your left hand, left knee and left 
lower leg despite the high dose steroid medication.  Your left 
hand improved, but your left knee and lower left leg began to 
bruise. We were concerned that your left lower leg might be 
infected, and we kept you in the hospital to monitor your 
symptoms.  Your leg improved, and you will be able to go home 
without antibiotics and with a slow decrease (taper) of your 
oral steroid medication called prednisone.

Continued to take all of your medications as you were taking 
them prior to admission, with the following change.

70mg (7 tabs) per day for one week; 60mg (6tabs) per day for one

___.

THREE VIEWS OF THE LEFT KNEE: Extensive soft tissue edema and small
suprapatellar joint effusion.  No acute fracture or subluxation.  No erosive
or suspicious lytic or sclerotic osseous lesion.   No soft tissue
calcification or radiopaque foreign body.  Skin staples have been removed.

NONVASCULAR LOWER EXTREMITY ULTRASOUND 

INDICATION:  ___ man with psoriatic arthritis and on immunomodulatory
therapy.  Now with increasing pain in left calf surrounding the scar.

FINDINGS:  A linear transducer was used to scan the area of the scar.  There
is a hypoechoic scar tissue, but there is no evidence of focal fluid
collections.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of fluid collection at the area of scar in the left
calf.

INDICATION:  ___ male with history of psoriatic arthritis and prior
leg calf abscess status post I+D, now on high-dose IV steroids for arthritic
flare.  Evaluate for osteonecrosis of the left knee.

COMPARISON:  ___ and ___ and MRIs of the ___ and ___.  MRI of the knee dated ___ was also reviewed.

TECHNIQUE:  MR imaging of the left knee was performed per standard department
protocol, including axial proton density fat saturated images, sagittal proton
density images, sagittal T2 fat saturated images, and coronal proton density
fat saturated images.  No contrast was administered.

FINDINGS:

Soft tissue deformity and edema medially, involving the medial head of
gastrocnemius muscle, is consistent with the sequelae of prior incision and
drainage of medial calf abscess.  There is no new or residual fluid collection
identified.

There is a moderate-to-large right knee joint effusion.  There is synovial
thickening again in keeping with synovitis. There is a small ___ cyst.

In the patellofemoral compartment, there is full-thickness cartilage loss,
particularly involving the medial patellar facet, with additional thinning
involving the lateral patellar facet.  There is associated cartilage thinning
in the trochlea.  There is resultant subchondral marrow edema and cystic
change in the patella.

There is thinning and fraying of articular cartilage in the medial
compartment, with marginal osteophyte formation, in keeping with degenerative
change.  There is some marrow edema identified in the medial femoral condyle,
likely degenerative/reactive.  The cortical surfaces are intact.

There is mild cartilage thinning in the lateral compartment, without
full-thickness cartilage loss.  Small marginal osteophytes are also noted.

The lateral meniscus is normal in morphology and signal intensity, without
evidence for lateral meniscus tear.  However, there is an obliquely oriented
tear within the body and posterior horn of the medial meniscus.

The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments are intact and normal in
appearance.  The lateral collateral ligament complex is intact.  The medial
collateral ligament is intact, though there is some edema about the medial
collateral ligament, likely reactive secondary to prior surgical intervention
and inflammation.

There is high signal identified within the extensor mechanism, including
within the patellar tendon at its proximal and distal insertions, as well as
within the distal aspect of the quadriceps tendon.  Additional edema in the
deep infrapatellar bursa.  There is also high signal within the suprapatellar
fat pad, compatible with impingement.  There is mild prepatellar edema.

Other than degenerative marrow edema in the medial femoral condyle and in the
patella, there is no marrow signal abnormality to suggest osteonecrosis.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence for osteonecrosis of the left knee.

2.  Obliquely oriented tear involving the body and posterior horn of the
medial meniscus.

3.  Tricompartmental degenerative change, with cartilage fraying in the medial
and lateral compartments, and full-thickness cartilage loss in the
patellofemoral compartment.  There is associated marrow edema and subchondral
cystic change within the medial femoral condyle and within the patella.

4.  Moderate-to-large joint effusion and small ___ cyst.

5.  Persistent signal abnormality and soft tissue distortion within the medial
aspect of the knee and medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle, compatible
with surgical history, without focal collection to suggest persistent or
recurrent abscess.
